title: When Gloucestershire Appeared on Iran’s Map
author: Peter Bach
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Gloucestershire_UK_locator_map_2010.svg-680x497.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/29/when-
gloucestershire-appeared-on-irans-map/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Gloucestershire_UK_locator_map_2010.svg-680x497.png)

Image Source: Nilfanion - Ordnance Survey OpenData - [CC BY-SA
3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)

There was something oddly disorientating about hearing the Islamic
Revolutionary Guard Corps mention RAF Fairford last week.

Fairford is hardly a place that intrudes on the world’s imagination. I spend
Christmas not far from there. That is my only connection. Most people know it,
if they know it at all, for the Royal International Air Tattoo, or as a sleepy
corner of Gloucestershire surrounded by fields, stone villages and long, quiet
roads.

Yet last week the IRGC, through Iran’s official news agency, declared that any
military base used to launch attacks on Iran would be considered a “legitimate
target”. It specifically named Fairford, claiming American B-1 bombers had
flown missions against Iran from there.

The UK government insists it is simply maintaining the long-standing
arrangement that allows US forces to operate from certain UK bases, while also
maintaining that the UK is not itself participating in offensive operations
against Iran. It is an increasingly fine distinction, particularly as Donald
Trump continues to criticise European allies, including the UK, for not doing
enough to support the United States.

Following the Iranian warning, ministers said the UK’s armed forces stood
ready to defend the country and any military installations under threat.
Whether Fairford is genuinely at risk is almost beside the point.

At around the same time, reports emerged that individuals linked to Iranian
intelligence had attempted to enter the UK on small boats, with claims
focusing on the IRGC’s Unit 700, the logistics branch that supports the Quds
Force’s covert overseas operations. Some questioned why intelligence
operatives would choose such a route rather than entering through more
conventional means. Yet that objection is not conclusive. For much of the past
decade, Iranians have consistently ranked among the largest national groups
claiming asylum in the UK, meaning their presence among Channel crossings is
not, in itself, evidence of intelligence activity.

Iran itself is harder still to contemplate. Only days ago the country endured
sustained military operations and nightly strikes. For a brief period, it
appeared the conflict might be settling into an uneasy pause. That impression
has now evaporated. Over the past forty-eight hours, Iranian missiles were
launched towards American forces in the region, while drones targeted Saudi
energy infrastructure. According to US Central Command, all missiles directed
at American positions were intercepted. In response, American and Saudi
aircraft carried out coordinated strikes against Iran-aligned militia sites in
Iraq, marking a significant widening of the conflict beyond direct US-Iran
exchanges.

Wars often do this. They do not merely grow. They become normal. What seemed
extraordinary one week becomes routine the next. That is the nightmare for
everyone involved.

Iran now appears caught in exactly that transition: from sporadic
confrontation to sustained war. Even from afar, there is a growing sense that
no one quite knows where to look.

In an interview with Christiane Amanpour, Tina Brown argued that “Trump has no
one with him who remotely understands the Iranian mindset. The Iranians
understand Trump far better than he understands them.” Others dispute that
assessment, but the wider concern remains the same: miscalculation is becoming
increasingly dangerous.

Any hope that the fighting was settling into a stable pause has proved
premature. The latest exchange of missile attacks, drone strikes and
retaliatory operations demonstrates how quickly even a temporary lull can give
way to renewed escalation. Rather than moving towards de-escalation, the
conflict increasingly resembles a regional confrontation involving multiple
state and proxy actors operating across Iraq, Jordan, the Gulf and the Red
Sea.

Iran had responded previously with missiles and drones directed at American
and allied positions in Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq, while Iran-backed
Houthi attacks had continued to disrupt shipping in the Red Sea as part of the
so-called Axis of Resistance. All sides continue to make battlefield claims
that cannot yet be independently verified.

Iraq has once again become one of the principal theatres of the conflict.
Following attempted attacks attributed by Washington to Iran-backed militias,
reports indicated that US and Saudi forces jointly struck logistics and
weapons sites used by those groups. If confirmed, the operation would mark
Saudi Arabia’s most direct military role alongside the United States after
months of attempting to avoid being drawn fully into the conflict.

Perhaps the most reliable measure of a war is not the number of missiles that
fall, but the number of ordinary lives made smaller by it. Bridges are
damaged. Electricity falters. Families are displaced. Independent reporting
grows ever more difficult. Political prisoners disappear further from view.
These quieter consequences have a terrible habit of outlasting the fighting
itself.

Shipping insurance premiums have risen again, commercial vessels—where they
can sail safely—continue to alter their routes, energy markets remain
volatile, and governments across the region are preparing for a conflict that
no one seems confident can still be contained.

International concern has intensified. The UN Secretary-General has warned the
crisis is “getting out of control”, while governments across the Middle East
have strengthened military preparedness and issued fresh travel advisories.
Even Ukraine found itself accused at the weekend of attacking an Iranian
vessel in the Caspian Sea—an allegation that, regardless of its accuracy,
illustrates how quickly the conflict is spilling into new diplomatic and
strategic arenas.

Inside Iran itself, attention has turned to the country’s leadership. The
principal uncertainty surrounds Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who was
seriously injured earlier in the war and has yet to make a public appearance
or broadcast. President Masoud Pezeshkian has said communication with him is
increasing, but his prolonged absence has only reinforced the perception that
the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is exercising greater influence over
wartime decision-making.

Diplomatic contacts continue through regional intermediaries, but they have
produced no durable breakthrough. Iranian officials have participated in
mediation while publicly rejecting American pressure, and the renewed exchange
of attacks suggests the previous interim ceasefire has effectively collapsed.

Iran has also accused Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner of exploiting
confidential information obtained during the US-Iran negotiations to profit
from market movements during the conflict. The White House strongly denied the
allegation, and no independent evidence has yet emerged to substantiate it.

An Iranian Health Ministry official has reported 53 civilians killed and 592
wounded since late June, although those totals cannot yet be independently
verified. Damage to bridges, electricity infrastructure and other essential
services is increasing the risks faced by civilians, while the United Nations
has expressed concern about attacks on civilian infrastructure across the
region. Human rights organisations also warn that wartime conditions are
enabling intensified repression, arbitrary detention and greater risks for
political prisoners.

The broader conflict has reportedly killed thousands—primarily in Iran and
Lebanon—and displaced millions since February. Those figures continue to rise
as the fighting spreads.

The quiet that briefly descended now appears to have been less the beginning
of peace than the pause between phases of the same conflict. The latest
attacks on American forces, the joint US-Saudi strikes in Iraq, and the
continued activity of Iranian-backed militias all suggest that the war is
becoming broader rather than narrower. Each new participant adds another layer
of complexity to a conflict that is increasingly difficult to contain.

When the IRGC named RAF Fairford, it was tempting to treat the warning as
rhetorical. Yet as the conflict expands across Iraq, Jordan, Saudi Arabia and
the Gulf, the list of places drawn into its geography continues to grow.
Fairford no longer feels like an isolated footnote. It is one point on an
increasingly crowded map.

Whether or not another B-1 bomber ever leaves RAF Fairford for Iran is, in
some ways, the least important part of the story. What matters is that an
English airfield now occupies a place in the mental geography of a Middle
Eastern conflict whose future remains uncertain.

For those living in Iran, even brief moments of quiet offer relief rather than
reassurance. Homes remain damaged, families remain displaced, political
prisoners remain hidden from view, and no one can say with confidence whether
the next lull marks the beginning of diplomacy or merely the interval before
another round of fighting. That, more than the movement of aircraft or the
drawing of military maps, remains the true measure of the conflict.
